# Producer–Consumer Fairness Sandbox

Chapter 7's asynchronous producer&ndash;consumer example (`ex:prod-cons`) has a two-cell shared buffer. At each step, the scheduler runs *at most one* of the two processes; the other remains idle. This notebook lets you be the scheduler.

- **Producer** fills the leftmost empty cell.
- **Consumer** always empties cell 0; it keeps cell 1 only if cell 0 was non-empty just before running.

The property to watch is $\mathbf{G}(\mathit{full} \to \mathbf{F}(\mathit{empty\_cell}))$: *whenever the buffer is full, some cell is eventually freed.* Without fairness, this is false&mdash;and you can build the exact schedule that breaks it.

```{=html}
<script>
(function() {
  let buffer = ['empty', 'empty'];
  let schedule = [];
  let objCounter = 0;
  let sinceLastFree = 0; // consecutive steps the buffer has been full, right after the step
  const STARVE_THRESHOLD = 5;

  function nextLabel() {
    objCounter = (objCounter % 3) + 1;
    return 'o' + objCounter;
  }

  function producerEnabled(buf) { return buf.includes('empty'); }
  function consumerEnabled(buf) { return buf.some(c => c !== 'empty'); }
  function isFull(buf) { return buf[0] !== 'empty' && buf[1] !== 'empty'; }

  function producerStep(buf) {
    const b0 = buf[0], b1 = buf[1];
    const label = nextLabel();
    const n0 = b0 === 'empty' ? label : b0;
    const n1 = (b0 !== 'empty' && b1 === 'empty') ? label : b1;
    return [n0, n1];
  }

  function consumerStep(buf) {
    const b0 = buf[0];
    const n0 = 'empty';
    const n1 = b0 !== 'empty' ? buf[1] : 'empty';
    return [n0, n1];
  }

  function runOne(kind) {
    buffer = kind === 'P' ? producerStep(buffer) : consumerStep(buffer);
    schedule.push(kind);
    sinceLastFree = isFull(buffer) ? sinceLastFree + 1 : 0;
    render();
  }

  function runProducerTen() {
    for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) runOne('P');
  }

  function reset() {
    buffer = ['empty', 'empty'];
    schedule = [];
    objCounter = 0;
    sinceLastFree = 0;
    render();
  }

  function render() {
    const bufEl = document.getElementById('nb26-buffer');
    bufEl.innerHTML = '';
    buffer.forEach((c, i) => {
      const div = document.createElement('div');
      div.className = 'fs-cell' + (c !== 'empty' ? ' filled' : '');
      div.textContent = c === 'empty' ? '—' : c;
      bufEl.appendChild(div);
    });

    const pEn = producerEnabled(buffer), cEn = consumerEnabled(buffer);
    document.getElementById('nb26-badges').innerHTML = `
      <span class="fs-badge ${pEn ? 'enabled' : 'disabled'}">producer enabled: ${pEn}</span>
      <span class="fs-badge ${cEn ? 'enabled' : 'disabled'}">consumer enabled: ${cEn}</span>
    `;

    const warnEl = document.getElementById('nb26-warning');
    if (sinceLastFree >= STARVE_THRESHOLD) {
      warnEl.innerHTML = `<div class="fs-warning-box fs-warning-bad">Buffer has stayed full for ${sinceLastFree} consecutive steps. Keep running only the Producer and this is exactly the unfair run from Example (fairness in the producer&ndash;consumer): the scheduler always picks Producer, <code>consumer.running</code> is enabled at every step but never taken&mdash;this violates justice, and if it continued forever, G(full &rarr; F(empty_cell)) would be false.</div>`;
    } else {
      warnEl.innerHTML = `<div class="fs-warning-box fs-warning-ok">No sustained starvation yet. (This notebook can only show a growing <em>finite</em> prefix&mdash;fairness itself is a property of the infinite continuation, exactly the caveat in the chapter.)</div>`;
    }

    const schedEl = document.getElementById('nb26-schedule');
    schedEl.innerHTML = '';
    schedule.forEach(k => {
      const span = document.createElement('span');
      span.className = 'fs-sched-step ' + k.toLowerCase();
      span.textContent = k;
      schedEl.appendChild(span);
    });
    schedEl.scrollTop = schedEl.scrollHeight;
  }

  document.getElementById('nb26-producer').addEventListener('click', () => runOne('P'));
  document.getElementById('nb26-consumer').addEventListener('click', () => runOne('C'));
  document.getElementById('nb26-producer10').addEventListener('click', runProducerTen);
  document.getElementById('nb26-reset').addEventListener('click', reset);

  render();
})();
</script>
```

## What to try

1. **Fill the buffer, then click "Run Producer ×10".** The buffer is already full, so every extra producer step changes nothing&mdash;but the warning box still fires, because `consumer.running` stays enabled (the buffer has a non-empty cell) and is never taken. That is exactly the justice violation from the chapter's fairness example: continued forever, this schedule refutes $\mathbf{G}(\mathit{full} \to \mathbf{F}(\mathit{empty\_cell}))$.
2. **Alternate Producer/Consumer by hand.** The buffer should never sit full for long, and the warning box should stay green.
3. **Notice what the badges track.** "Producer enabled" and "consumer enabled" are exactly the formal `Enabled` predicate from the chapter's fairness definitions (`def:enabled`)&mdash;a process being enabled is a fact about the *current* state, independent of whether the scheduler actually picks it.
